lessons.title: Clean it
lessons.job: Keep only the letters, in capitals, so counting and slicing see the cipher and nothing else.
lessons.intro: Spaces, punctuation and line breaks get in the way of counting letters and of cutting the text into pieces. A `for` loop looks at the text one character at a time; `if ch.isalpha():` keeps a character only when it is a letter. Once that is clear, the same thing fits on one line.

predict.question: What does this print?
predict.explain: The loop visits H, i, the comma, the space, T, o, m and the !. Only the five letters pass `isalpha()`, and each is added in capitals.

run.code:
ct = """OPLC LRYPD, ESP WLXA TY ESP ZWO WTRSESZFDP HLD WTE
LRLTY WLDE YTRSE, ESZFRS YZMZOJ SLD WTGPO ESPCP
QZC EHPYEJ JPLCD. T CZHPO ZFE LE OLHY LYO QZFYO
QCPDS QZZEACTYED ZY ESP DELTCD LYO L WPEEPC ZY ESP
ELMWP, HCTEEPY TY L NZOP T OZ YZE VYZH. XPPE XP LE
ESP SLCMZFC ZY QCTOLJ LYO MCTYR JZFC YZEPMZZV. EZX"""

# 1. Remove every space and line break: split() cuts the text at them, join() glues the pieces
print("".join(ct.split()))

# 2. Keep only the letters, in capitals, one character at a time
t = ""
for ch in ct:
    if ch.isalpha():

lessons.title: Look at parts of it
lessons.job: Take pieces of the text by position: the start, the end, every fifth letter.
lessons.intro: Positions count from 0, and negative positions count from the end. A slice `t[a:b]` takes positions a up to (not including) b. The step slice `t[c::w]` takes every w-th letter, starting at position c: it is how you pull out the columns of a grid and the slices of a Vigenère text, so it is the most useful line in this whole course.

lessons.title: Print it in a grid
lessons.job: Write the text out in rows of a fixed width, to look for patterns that line up.
lessons.intro: Printing a text in rows of a fixed width is the first look at any transposition: at the right width, the rows line up and the columns show the pattern. `range(0, len(t), w)` counts 0, w, 2w, ... so each row starts where the last one ended. A transposition keeps every letter, so the right width usually divides the length exactly: `len(t) % w` is the remainder, and 0 means it divides.

predict.question: What does this print?
predict.explain: `i` takes the values 0, 4 and 8, so the slices are t[0:4], t[4:8] and t[8:12]. The last slice runs off the end, and a slice just stops there: IJ.

lessons.title: Read a grid by columns
lessons.job: Read the columns of a grid, top to bottom, as a columnar transposition does.
lessons.intro: A columnar transposition writes the message in rows and reads it off by columns. Column c of a grid of width w is the step slice `t[c::w]`: one letter from every row. A list holds several values in order, and a list comprehension builds one in a single line: `[t[i:i+w] for i in range(0, len(t), w)]` is the list of rows.

predict.question: What does this print?
predict.explain: In rows of three the grid is ABC, DEF, GHI. `t[0::3]` takes positions 0, 3 and 6, which is the first column, ADG; then BEH and CFI.

run.code:

ENAOH BURWL RLBAI ARGTN RAOHN CCEDM AOOXL EXN"""
t = "".join(ch for ch in ct if ch.isalpha()).upper()
w = 6

rows = [t[i:i+w] for i in range(0, len(t), w)]
print(rows[:3])          # the first three rows, as a list
for c in range(w):

lessons.title: Rearrange columns
lessons.job: Put the letters of every row back in order with a key: the way to undo a block transposition.
learn: a list of numbers as a key
indexing with each number in a list
joining letters in a new order
lessons.intro: A block transposition shuffles every row of the grid the same way. The key to undo it is a list of positions: `order = [2, 0, 1]` means take letter 2 of the row, then letter 0, then letter 1. A columnar transposition, written in rows and read off by columns, is undone by cutting the text into equal columns and reading across them.

lessons.title: Look for a crib or a name
lessons.job: Check which expected words appear in a text, how often, and where.
lessons.intro: A crib is a word you expect in the message: a name, DEAR at the start, a sign-off at the end. Once part of a cipher is undone, or to check a guessed decryption, Python can look for every word on a list at once. `in` answers yes or no, `count` says how often, and `find` says where (or -1 when the word is not there).

lessons.title: Measure: the index of coincidence
lessons.job: Work out the index of coincidence, which tells one alphabet from several.
learn: sum() over a loop in brackets
lessons.intro: The index of coincidence (IoC) is the chance that two letters picked at random from the text are the same. English, and anything that only relabels or moves its letters (Caesar, substitution, transposition), is about 0.066; letters spread evenly over all 26 give about 0.038. A Vigenère cipher sits in between, and its slices `t[c::w]` look like English again at the right width. The formula is: for each letter, its count n times (n - 1), all added up, divided by N times (N - 1), where N is the length.

predict.question: What does this print?
predict.explain: A gives 2 × 1 = 2 and B gives 1 × 0 = 0, so the top is 2; the bottom is 3 × 2 = 6. 2 / 6 is a third, which Python prints with all its digits.

lessons.title: Letters as numbers
lessons.job: Turn letters into numbers and back, so a shift is just adding and wrapping round.
lessons.intro: Every character has a number: `ord("A")` is 65, `ord("B")` is 66, and `chr` goes back. Subtract 65 and the alphabet is 0 to 25. Shifting is then adding, and `% 26` (the remainder after dividing by 26) wraps Z round to A. Caesar, affine and Vigenère all come down to this one line.

predict.question: What does this print?
predict.explain: Y is number 24. Add 3 to get 27, and 27 % 26 is 1, which is B. Without the `% 26`, `chr(27 + 65)` is a backslash: the character after Z in the computer's table.

run.code:
ct = """OPLC LRYPD, ESP WLXA TY ESP ZWO WTRSESZFDP HLD WTE
LRLTY WLDE YTRSE, ESZFRS YZMZOJ SLD WTGPO ESPCP
QZC EHPYEJ JPLCD. T CZHPO ZFE LE OLHY LYO QZFYO
QCPDS QZZEACTYED ZY ESP DELTCD LYO L WPEEPC ZY ESP
ELMWP, HCTEEPY TY L NZOP T OZ YZE VYZH. XPPE XP LE
ESP SLCMZFC ZY QCTOLJ LYO MCTYR JZFC YZEPMZZV. EZX"""
t = "".join(ch for ch in ct if ch.isalpha()).upper()

k = 3   # shift back by k
out = ""
for ch in t[:40]:
    x = ord(ch) - ord("A")          # A=0, B=1, ... Z=25
    out = out + chr((x - k) % 26 + ord("A"))
print(t[:40])
print(out)

lessons.title: Keep a tool
lessons.job: Wrap a job in a function, so one line runs it on any text with any key.
learn: map(), and why it needs list() or join()
lessons.intro: A function is a tool with a name. `def shift(text, k):` says what it needs; `return` hands back the answer. lessons.title: Three imports worth knowing
lessons.job: Three one-line helpers from Python's standard library, once the long way is clear.
lessons.intro: Everything so far used built-ins only, on purpose: you can read every line. Python also comes with a standard library, and three of its tools save real work. `Counter` counts in one line; `textwrap.wrap` cuts a text into rows; `permutations` lists every order of some columns, which turns "look" into "search": try all 720 orders of 6 columns and print only those that contain a crib. It is still your own code.

run.code:
from collections import Counter
from itertools import permutations
import textwrap

ct = """HETKY ESDIN EUTTR EHHRT ISODE ONRMF HETLF EOHTT
ENAOH BURWL RLBAI ARGTN RAOHN CCEDM AOOXL EXN"""
t = "".join(ch for ch in ct if ch.isalpha()).upper()

print(Counter(t).most_common(5))     # lesson 8 and 9 in one line
print(textwrap.wrap(t, 6)[:4])       # lesson 4's rows, as a list

# Every order of the 6 columns: keep the ones that make HARBOUR appear
for order in permutations(range(6)):
    plain = "".join(t[i + k] for i in range(0, len(t), 6) for k in order)
    if "HARBOUR" in plain:
        print(order, plain[:30])
